samples.summary: Browser OAuth `state` is an unauthenticated double-submit cookie with no `__Host-` prefix and no server-side binding, so a sibling-subdomain foothold restores login CSRF
samples.evidence: `oauthStateCookieOptions()` sets `wafflebase_oauth_state` with `path:'/auth'` and no `__Host-` prefix (oauth-state.ts:57-68), and `webOAuthStateMatches` accepts any `state` whose SHA-256 preimage happens to be in that cookie (oauth-state.ts:47-55). The value is a bare random secret, not an HMAC over anything the server can re-derive. Cookie tossing is therefore the whole attack: an attacker who controls or XSSes ANY sibling host under the registrable domain (e.g. `blog.example.com`, a staging host, a takeover-able CNAME) sets `Set-Cookie: wafflebase_oauth_state=<their secret>; Domain=example.com; Path=/auth`, then navigates the victim to `/auth/github/callback?code=<code minted for the ATTACKER's GitHub account>&state=web.<sha256(their secret)>`. auth.controller.ts:148-159 finds a match, falls through to line 189-192, and issues `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` for the attacker's account in the victim's browser — the exact session-fixation the change set out to close. `__Host-` prefixing (which forbids `Domain=` and forces `Path=/`), or making `state` an HMAC over a server secret, removes the cookie-tossing degree of freedom. The same applies to `wafflebase_cli_confirm` (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:33-41), whose secret is likewise only proven by cookie possession.

samples.summary: Any cross-site subresource load of `GET /auth/github` overwrites a victim's in-flight OAuth state cookie, cancelling their login (CSRF-triggered login denial)
samples.evidence: `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` unconditionally does `res.cookie(OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE, secret, ...)` for every non-CLI request to `/auth/github` (github-auth.guard.ts:64-68). The cookie has one fixed name and path, so it is single-slot. `SameSite=Lax` governs whether a cookie is *sent*, not whether `Set-Cookie` on a cross-site response is *stored*. An attacker page can therefore emit `` (or a `no-cors` fetch) while the victim is sitting on GitHub's consent screen; the response's `Set-Cookie` replaces the victim's secret. When the victim consents, `webOAuthStateMatches` fails at auth.controller.ts:157 and they are bounced to `/login?error=oauth_state`. Repeating this on a loop makes GitHub sign-in permanently impossible for any user who visits the attacker's page. A per-attempt cookie name/keyed store, or accepting a small set of pending states, would avoid the single-slot clobber.

samples.summary: The CLI confirmation secret is described as single-use but is only browser-enforced — the server keeps no record, so the same `confirm=`/cookie pair can be replayed indefinitely
samples.evidence: `res.clearCookie(CLI_CONFIRM_COOKIE, ...)` (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:71-74) is the entire single-use enforcement, and it is an instruction to the client. The middleware compares the query `confirm` value to whatever cookie the request carries and keeps no server-side ledger of spent secrets. Any non-browser client (or a browser the attacker controls) can replay `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=…&nonce=…&confirm=S` with `Cookie: wafflebase_cli_confirm=S` for the cookie's full 5-minute window, each time minting a fresh `CliAuthStore` state entry. The comment at line 71-72 ("Single use: … it is spent here rather than left to be replayed") overstates the property, which matters because it is the load-bearing claim of the CSRF gate documented in docs/design/rest-api.md.

samples.summary: `findOrCreateUser` runs before the OAuth `state` check, so a refused / CSRF'd callback still provisions a user record
samples.evidence: auth.controller.ts:115-120 upserts the user unconditionally; the state validation that decides whether the callback is legitimate does not begin until line 144. A callback carrying no `state`, a mismatched `state`, or an expired CLI token therefore still writes a `User` row before being refused at lines 145/158/183. An attacker replaying codes obtained for accounts they control can seed user records at will (bounded only by the 10/min throttle on line 106). Moving the upsert below the state check would make the refusal actually inert.

samples.summary: `LOGIN_ERRORS[error]` is an unguarded prototype-chain lookup on attacker-controlled query input, so `?error=constructor` yields a function as a React child
samples.evidence: `error` comes straight from `useSearchParams().get("error")` (login/page.tsx:49) and is used as an object index at login-form.tsx:32. `LOGIN_ERRORS` is a plain object literal, so `LOGIN_ERRORS['constructor']`, `['toString']`, `['valueOf']`, `['hasOwnProperty']` all resolve to inherited functions — truthy, so the `??` fallback to `GENERIC_LOGIN_ERROR` never fires and `message` becomes a function rendered as a React child. A link such as `https://app/login?error=constructor` therefore breaks the sign-in page for anyone who follows it (React refuses function children). Note packages/frontend has no `tsc` lane, so this is not caught mechanically. Use `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(LOGIN_ERRORS, error)`, a `Map`, or a null-prototype object.

samples.summary: The CLI `nonce` is optional, so the backend will redirect a freshly minted auth code to an attacker-chosen loopback port with no binding at all
samples.evidence: `parseCliNonce(req.query?.nonce)` returns `undefined` for a missing or malformed nonce (github-auth.guard.ts:16-19, 61) and `createState` accepts it (cli-auth.store.ts:27-43). In the callback, `state.nonce` being falsy produces `stateParam = ''` (auth.controller.ts:173-175), so the redirect is `http://127.0.0.1:<attacker-chosen port>/callback?code=…` with no `state`. Combined with a user who clicks Continue on an attacker-supplied confirmation page (`?mode=cli&port=<any 1024-65535>` — the middleware forwards whatever port it was handed, cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:100-103), any process already listening on that loopback port on the victim's machine receives a code it can trade at the unauthenticated `POST /auth/cli/exchange` (auth.controller.ts:195-211) for full access/refresh tokens for the victim. Now that the shipped CLI always sends a nonce, requiring it (and rejecting the CLI flow when it is absent or malformed rather than silently degrading) removes the unbound variant.

samples.summary: The CLI confirmation page sets XFO/CSP/Referrer-Policy but not `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`
samples.evidence: cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:80-84 sets `X-Frame-Options`, `frame-ancestors`, `Cache-Control`, `Referrer-Policy` and `Content-Type`, but no `nosniff`. This is the one HTML document the backend origin serves, and it embeds a one-time secret; adding `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` (and ideally a restrictive `Content-Security-Policy` beyond `frame-ancestors`, since the page carries an inline `<style>`) costs nothing. I grepped the backend for `setHeader('X-Content-Type-Options'` and for a helmet registration in main.ts/app.module.ts and found none.

samples.summary: Security doc states the callback answers a stateless request with a 400; the code redirects to the login page instead
samples.evidence: rest-api.md:355 says "requires a `state` on **every** path; a callback without one is a 400, never a sign-in", but auth.controller.ts:144-146 returns `res.redirect(this.loginErrorUrl('oauth_state'))` (a 302), and the mismatched-state path at line 158 does the same. Only the CLI-token-invalid branch (line 183) still throws `BadRequestException`. Threat-model docs that misdescribe the enforced behaviour mislead the next person auditing this flow; nested/behavioural doc drift is not caught by the top-level docs link check.

finding.summary: Browser OAuth `state` is an unauthenticated double-submit cookie with no `__Host-` prefix and no server-side binding, so a sibling-subdomain foothold restores login CSRF
finding.evidence: `oauthStateCookieOptions()` sets `wafflebase_oauth_state` with `path:'/auth'` and no `__Host-` prefix (oauth-state.ts:57-68), and `webOAuthStateMatches` accepts any `state` whose SHA-256 preimage happens to be in that cookie (oauth-state.ts:47-55). verdict.reason: All claimed code is present as described. OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE = 'wafflebase_oauth_state' (oauth-state.ts:20) has no __Host- prefix, and oauthStateCookieOptions() (oauth-state.ts:57-68) sets path:'/auth' with no domain/host binding, so the cookie is not host-locked. createWebOAuthState (oauth-state.ts:35-38) mints a bare randomBytes(32) secret and webOAuthStateMatches (oauth-state.ts:47-55 with hashSecret at 78-80) accepts any state equal to 'web.'+sha256(cookieSecret) - there is no HMAC over a server secret and no server-side state record for the web flow (the design comment at oauth-state.ts:8-14 explicitly rejects a server-side map), so the server cannot distinguish a state/secret pair it minted from one an attacker minted. The callback reads the cookie at auth.controller.ts:152, accepts at 157, and falls through to createTokens/setAuthCookies at 189-192, issuing wafflebase_session/wafflebase_refresh for whichever GitHub account the presented code belongs to - session fixation. I searched for a mitigating guard and found none: cookies are unsigned (github-auth.guard.ts:66 passes no signed option), sameSite:'lax' is deliberate (oauth-state.ts:61-64) so the cookie IS sent on the cross-site callback navigation, and no domain restriction or origin check exists. An attacker controlling any sibling host under the registrable domain can set Domain=eTLD+1; Path=/auth and, because that cookie is created before the victim's legitimate one, RFC 6265 ordering makes it the value cookie-parser surfaces at auth.controller.ts:152. cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:33-41 and 66-76 have the identical shape for wafflebase_cli_confirm. This is a weakened CSRF/auth verification, squarely in the security lens; no refutation ground applies - it is not absent, no guard makes it unreachable, and it is not out of lane.

finding.summary: Reviewer did not produce a valid verdict: review: every credential in the pool (3) was retired — nothing left to fail over to

verdict.reason: The finding is not a claim about repository code at all — it is the review harness's own infrastructure error surfaced as a finding ("Reviewer did not produce a valid verdict: ..."). The quoted string is verbatim the message constructed by poolExhaustedError() at scripts/agent/ask.mjs:630-637, which is thrown (kind "pool-exhausted", retryable false) when the agent's credential pool is drained; the security lens agent aborted before emitting a verdict. The item names no file, no line, no code construct, and no attack vector, so there is nothing present-as-described to verify. I additionally inspected the cited code region for a real in-lane issue: the error message interpolates only `label` and the integer `pool.size` — no token, key, or credential material is embedded or logged (ask.mjs:630-636), and the surrounding comments (ask.mjs:622-628) document deliberately withholding the per-slot reason and deferring "which secret" to a separate auth smoke check, so there is no secret-exposure defect here either. The repository's own retrospective independently classifies this exact message as an infrastructure failure with no code signal (docs/tasks/active/20260806-cli-status-ctx-structured-output-lessons.md:272-280). This is not a blocking security defect; it indicates the security review did not run, which is a harness/re-run concern rather than a merge-gate code finding.
